items.title: Spotlight Now: Hawaii's $25,000 'price of paradise' earning gap is driving residents away
items.description:
UHERO economist Carl Bonham warns that Hawaiʻi's $25,000 real earning power gap compared to the mainland will widen to $35,000 by 2035, fueling out-migration.

For more Local News from Hawaii News Now: https:/www.hawaiinewsnow.com
For more YouTube Content: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCBnLE14tUHTDyDc8Xij9rAg
items.why_watch: UHERO economist Carl Bonham lays out a specific, data-driven case for why Hawaii's cost-of-living gap isn't just painful now — it's structurally worsening, with real earning power projected to fall $10,000 further behind the mainland by 2035. If you've ever wondered why people actually leave paradise, this replaces the vague "it's expensive" narrative with hard numbers and economic mechanics. At 32 minutes it's a proper deep-dive, not a headline grab.

That’s what a new peer-reviewed study published in Earth’s Future has done, and […] The post Climate attribution science just changed the rules for fossil fuel lawsuits first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

discovery_articles.title: ‘Night of the Living Dead’ Grave Markers in Evans City, Pennsylvania
discovery_articles.snippet: The filming location and featured grave markers from George A. Romero's 1968 horror masterpiece, “Night of the Living Dead.” Includes Nicholas Kramer's grave, a civil war veteran who's headstone is shown during the delivery of famous line "They're coming to get you, Barbra!" Also the Blair / Cole plot where Johnny and Barbra stop to honor their father. And finally, the grave of Clyde Lewis Meyers, where Johnny hits his head during his tussle with one of the zombies (ghouls).
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The gravestones in Romero's zombie classic belonged to real people — including a Civil War veteran whose headstone became the backdrop for one of horror cinema's most iconic lines. There's something quietly uncanny about the fact that Nicholas Kramer's actual resting place is now forever part of the undead canon.

discovery_articles.title: The Birdhouse Tree of Riga in Rīga, Latvia
discovery_articles.snippet: In Riga’s elegant Esplanāde, one bare tree stands out from the surrounding greenery. Its trunk and branches are crowded with scores of small wooden birdhouses, painted in an assortment of greens, yellows, reds, pinks and natural tones. From below, the collection is so dense that the boxes can initially resemble an unusual lighting installation.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A single leafless tree in a Latvian park has been so densely colonized by handmade birdhouses that visitors mistake it for a light installation — which feels like the most charming possible case of mistaken identity.

discovery_articles.title: Adam’s Gulch  in Ketchum, Idaho
discovery_articles.snippet: Mountain bikers and hikers pour into Adam’s Gulch for its 33 miles of interconnected trails, but the gulch has a quieter claim to attention: more than a century ago, it was home to an early ranger station in what became the Ketchum Ranger District. After the Sawtooth National Forest was established in 1905, its territory was divided into ranger districts, with the first ranger’s station at Adam’s Gulch built in 1909. The district’s administrative center later moved elsewhere, leaving the gulch to become better known for recreation than bureaucracy.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Before mountain bikers claimed these Idaho trails as their own, the gulch quietly hosted one of the earliest ranger stations in a brand-new national forest — bureaucracy planted in wilderness, then politely forgotten.

discovery_articles.title: Silver Creek Preserve in Bellevue, Idaho
discovery_articles.snippet: In the high desert near Picabo, Idaho, a cold, wildlife-filled stream winds through wetlands and grasslands, fed not primarily by mountain runoff but by water emerging from the ground. Water from the surrounding hills and nearby Big Wood River percolates underground through an aquifer before being forced back toward the surface near the Picabo Hills. Numerous springs feed seven large tributaries of Silver Creek.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Silver Creek doesn't run down from the mountains like a well-behaved stream; it wells up from below, pushed to the surface through an aquifer like a secret the land has been keeping.

discovery_articles.title: Allergic to Dogs? These Gene-Edited Beagles Could Pave the Way to Your Dream Canine Companion That Won't Trigger Sniffles
discovery_articles.snippet: Geneticists altered Alfie and Bailey’s DNA so that they don't produce a major allergen. However, canines like them are not currently commercially available, and some experts express ethical concerns about altering the animals' genes
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Two beagles named Alfie and Bailey have had a single allergen quietly snipped from their DNA — a small edit that could mean a great deal to the estimated 10–20% of people who love dogs from a wheezing distance.

discovery_articles.title: This 91-Year-Old Man Fell 71 Times While Hiking the Appalachian Trail. He Just Became the Oldest Person to Complete the 2,190-Mile Trek
discovery_articles.snippet: Dale Sanders finished the hike in just under a year. Nicknamed "Grey Beard," he's no stranger to age-defying feats of endurance
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Dale Sanders fell 71 times over 2,190 miles and still crossed the finish line at 91 — which suggests that 'Grey Beard' has a rather different relationship with the concept of stopping than most of us do.

discovery_articles.title: Female Treefrogs Experience 'Choice Overload' Amid Too Many Mating Calls From Males
discovery_articles.snippet: Faced with a chorus of potential mates, female Cope’s gray treefrogs may be overwhelmed by the number of options and struggle to make a careful decision, a study suggests
discovery_articles.ferns_note: It turns out female treefrogs suffer from the same paradox of choice that derails humans in streaming queues and restaurant menus — too many crooning options, and the careful decision simply doesn't get made.

discovery_articles.title: We’ve Been Strapping Cargo to Our Backs for Millions of Years, but Backpack Innovation Really Took Off Around the Civil War
discovery_articles.snippet: Discover the origin story for an accessory being comfortably lugged by nearly every hiker and student, with about 450 million sold each year
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Humans have been slinging loads onto their backs for millions of years, yet the humble backpack as we know it didn't really find its form until soldiers needed a smarter way to carry their lives into battle during the Civil War.
